title: Yudhishthira in hell
hook: Yudhishthira reaches heaven, finds his old enemy enthroned there, and goes looking for his family
carry: heaven and hell are stops, not the end
tomorrow: why would God need to be born at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dog at heaven's gate turned out to be Dharma, and Yudhishthira had refused to leave it. Your line was the divine in every creature, even a dog.

The chariot sets him down in heaven, and the first face Yudhishthira sees is Duryodhana's. The cousin behind the rigged game of dice. The man who had Draupadi dragged into the hall. The one who would not make peace. He sits in splendor, honored among the gods. Yudhishthira's brothers are nowhere. Draupadi is nowhere. Karna is nowhere. And the man who refused heaven's chariot rather than abandon a dog says, in effect, that he does not want this heaven. Take me to my brothers. Wherever they are, that's where I want to be.
screen: `DURYODHANA, ENTHRONED.` → `NO BROTHERS. NO DRAUPADI.` → `"TAKE ME TO THEM."`

segments.voice: The sage Narada tries to calm him: old quarrels end here, and Duryodhana died fighting as a warrior. Yudhishthira won't be calmed. So the gods send a messenger to guide him to his family. The path turns dark and smells of decay. Thorns, burning things, a river that scalds. It is a hell. Yudhishthira turns to go back, and voices call out of the dark. Stay, they beg. While you stand here, a cool breeze blows and our pain eases. Who are you? Karna, they answer. Bhima. Arjuna. Nakula. Sahadeva. Dhrishtadyumna. Draupadi. Everyone he loved is in torment, while the man who caused the war sits on a throne. Yudhishthira is furious, at the gods and at dharma itself. Then he chooses: if his presence comforts them, he will stay in hell. And it ends. The gods appear, and the darkness lifts. It was an illusion, Indra explains; every king must glimpse hell, and Yudhishthira saw it for his own half-truth in the war, about Drona's son. He bathes in the heavenly Ganga and finds his family in their true forms. Now the teaching. In Hindu belief, svarga and naraka, heaven and hell, aren't forever. They're places karma passes through. Duryodhana's courage earned him heaven for a time; one half-truth earned Yudhishthira a glimpse of hell. The Gita says those who reach heaven by merit come back to earth when the merit runs out. The goal beyond both is moksha: freedom.
screen: `NARADA: OLD QUARRELS END HERE` · `VOICES IN THE DARK: "STAY"` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY IN HELL` · `THE ILLUSION LIFTS` · then, large: `HEAVEN AND HELL ARE STOPS; THE GOAL IS MOKSHA`

segments.voice: This is the end of a very long story, so give it a quiet minute. Think of one person who is going through a hard time right now. Send them a short message, nothing to fix, just that you're thinking of them. Yudhishthira couldn't end his family's pain; his being there was enough to cool the dark. If you pray, hold them in your prayer as you press send.
Svarga. Heaven, the realm Yudhishthira reaches, and then chooses to leave for the hell where his family waits.
Hold on to it: heaven and hell are stops, not the end. Tomorrow a new book opens, with a wedding and a sword. That's the end of a very long road.

howItsDone: The Svargarohana Parva is the last book of the Mahabharata, heard in recitations of the full epic. Its ending reflects a common Hindu belief: svarga and naraka are temporary, places karma passes through, and the final goal is moksha, freedom from the cycle of rebirth.

Duryodhana.meaning: the Kaurava cousin who would not make peace

Narada.meaning: a sage who appears across the epics and Puranas

Karna.meaning: the great warrior, the Pandavas' elder half-brother

Dhrishtadyumna.meaning: Draupadi's brother, a commander on the Pandava side

Ganga.meaning: the sacred river; here its heavenly stream

moksha.meaning: freedom from the cycle of birth and death, the final goal

naraka.meaning: hell, a place of suffering karma passes through
